quote: This work addresses the task of expanding abbreviated column names in tabular data... we formulate NAMEGUESS as a natural language generation problem.
Unlike previous textual abbreviation expansion works that formulated the task as a classification problem ... we formulate NAMEGUESS as a natural language generation problem.
we formulate NAMEGUESS as a natural language generation problem.
datasets: City Open Data, GitTables, WikiSQL, Dresden Web Table Corpus
outputs: expanded (logical) column names generated from abbreviated inputs
expanded column names from abbreviated forms

quote: We use three metrics for evaluation: exact match accuracy, F1 scores based on partial matches, and Bert F1 scores based on semantic matches.
We use three metrics for evaluation: exact match accuracy, F1 scores based on partial matches, and Bert F1 scores based on semantic matches.
We use three metrics for evaluation: exact match accuracy, F1 scores based on partial matches, and Bert F1 scores based on semantic matches.

The evaluation dataset was confirmed by 15 human annotators ... The annotators had access to 10 sampled cell values for each column. We also collected human performance from 6 annotators on 1,200 samples.
We collected human performance from 6 annotators on 1,200 samples from the evaluation set, including 300 from each difficulty level.
guideline: Annotators read table metadata and sampled cell values, determine if the original column name is abbreviated, and provide the well‑curated (expanded) variant.

Read the table metadata, including table category, name, and description. Read and understand the original column name and sampled cell values for that column. Determine if the original column name is abbreviated or well-curated. If in a well-curated form, provide only an 'abbreviated variant'. Otherwise, provide a 'well-curated variant' and an 'abbreviated variant'.
criteria: correctness of the expanded column name
